title: CAT Comparison, Link Criteria, and Local Globalization

items.title: Comparison triangles, the CAT(0) and CAT(1) inequalities, local CAT, local geodesics and round circles
items.statement:
Fix the following definitions and conventions for this page.

**(1) Models.** $\mathbb E^2$ is $\mathbb R^2$ with the Euclidean metric $d_2$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). The comparison sphere is $S^2\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the round metric $d_S(x,y):=\arccos(x\cdot y)$ ([[def-cg-spherical-gram-simplex-and-angular-link]], [[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]); more generally $d_S(x,y):=\arccos(x\cdot y)$ is defined on every sphere $S^{n-1}$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]).

**(2) Geodesic triangles and comparison.** A geodesic triangle in a metric space $X$ consists of three points $p,q,r\in X$ and a choice of geodesic segments $[p,q]$, $[q,r]$, $[r,p]$ joining them ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]); its perimeter is $d(p,q)+d(q,r)+d(r,p)$. A comparison triangle for it in $\mathbb E^2$, or in $S^2$ when its perimeter is $<2\pi$, is a triangle $(\bar p,\bar q,\bar r)$ in that model with the same three side lengths; it is unique up to an isometry of the model ([[lem-cg-comparison-convexity-and-model-spaces]]). For an occurrence of a point $x$ on a specified chosen side, the comparison point $\bar x$ is the point of the corresponding side of the comparison triangle at the same distance from the corresponding vertex; a vertex corresponds to itself. If a point belongs to more than one side, each side occurrence has its own comparison point, and the CAT inequalities quantify over every pair of side occurrences.

**(3) The CAT inequalities.** A metric space $X$ is **CAT(0)** if it is geodesic and for every geodesic triangle in $X$ and all points $x,y$ of that triangle, $d(x,y)\le d_2(\bar x,\bar y)$. It is **CAT(1)** if every pair of points of $X$ at distance $<D_1:=\pi$ is joined by a geodesic segment in $X$, and every geodesic triangle in $X$ of perimeter $<2\pi$ satisfies $d(x,y)\le d_S(\bar x,\bar y)$ for all points $x,y$ of the triangle. Thus for CAT(1) only triangles of perimeter $<2\pi$ are tested, and geodesic segments are demanded only for pairs at distance $<\pi$; a triangle of perimeter $<2\pi$ has all sides $<\pi$, so its sides are available by hypothesis. A metric space is **locally CAT(0)**, equivalently of curvature $\le0$, if every point has a closed ball $\bar B(x,r)$, $r>0$, such that the induced metric on $\bar B(x,r)$ is CAT(0); **locally CAT(1)** is defined in the same way.

**(4) Truncated angular metrics on links.** Let $F$ be a face of an isometric polyhedral gluing with its chain metric ([[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]]) and let $L:=\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$ be its angular link with the auxiliary extended componentwise path metric $d_{\mathrm{path}}$ and the finite angular metric $d_\pi:=\min\{\pi,d_{\mathrm{path}}\}$ ([[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]], [[lem-cg-spherical-simplex-existence-and-link-gram-formula]]). Then every $d_\pi$-triangle of perimeter $<2\pi$ has all sides $<\pi$: if one side were $\pi$, the triangle inequality would make the perimeter at least $2\pi$. Thus its vertices lie in one intrinsic component of $L$, and its side lengths equal the untruncated intrinsic path distances. It also holds between any two side points: the shorter of the two boundary routes has length at most half the perimeter, hence $<\pi$, so their truncated distance is $<\pi$ and equals their intrinsic path distance. Hence the CAT(1) tests in $(L,d_\pi)$ of perimeter $<2\pi$ agree with componentwise intrinsic tests ([[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]]). The empty metric space carries no triangles and satisfies the CAT(0) and CAT(1) tests vacuously; a one-point space is CAT(0) and CAT(1). With the conventions $C(\varnothing)=\{o\}$ and $L*\varnothing=L$ ([[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]]), the empty link satisfies the CAT(1) tests vacuously and its cone is a point.

**(5) Local geodesics.** Let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$ be an interval. A map $c:I\to X$ is a **constant-speed local geodesic** if there is a fixed $\lambda\ge0$ such that for every $t\in I$ some $\varepsilon>0$ satisfies $d(c(t'),c(t''))=\lambda|t'-t''|$ whenever $t',t''\in(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon)\cap I$. Here $\lambda$ is its speed; $\lambda=1$ is the unit-speed convention and $\lambda=0$ gives the constant paths. In this chapter “local geodesic” includes these linear reparametrizations. It is a **minimizing geodesic** precisely when the same distance equality holds for every pair $t',t''\in I$.

**(6) Length.** A continuous path $\gamma:[a,b]\to X$ has length $L(\gamma)\in[0,\infty]$, the supremum of its polygonal sums, and is rectifiable if $L(\gamma)<\infty$ ([[lem-cg-metric-target-length-reparametrization-and-lower-semicontinuity]], [[def-upper-bound]]). $X$ is a **length space** if for all $x,y\in X$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is a path from $x$ to $y$ of length $<d(x,y)+\varepsilon$.

**(7) Round circles.** For $\ell>0$ let $S^1_\ell:=\mathbb R/\ell\mathbb Z$ be the circle of circumference $\ell$, with $d_\ell(x,y):=\min\{|x-y+k\ell|:k\in\mathbb Z\}$; for $\ell=2\pi$ this is the unit circle. An **isometrically embedded circle of length $\ell$** in a metric space $X$ is an isometric embedding $S^1_\ell\to X$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]); its image is a subset of $X$ isometric to $(S^1_\ell,d_\ell)$.

items.title: Comparison angles of hinges, model triangle angles, and the Alexandrov upper angle
items.statement:
**(1) Comparison angle of a length triple.** For real lengths $b,c>0$ and $a\ge0$ satisfying $|b-c|\le a\le b+c$, define
$$\theta_E(a;b,c):=\arccos\!\left(\frac{b^2+c^2-a^2}{2bc}\right).$$
This is a number in $[0,\pi]$ ([[def-principal-inverse-sine-and-cosine]]): the two assumed length inequalities give $(b-c)^2\le a^2\le(b+c)^2$, hence $-2bc\le b^2+c^2-a^2\le2bc$. For spherical adjacent lengths $b,c\in(0,\pi)$ and an opposite length $a\ge0$, put
$$z_S(a;b,c):=\frac{\cos a-\cos b\cos c}{\sin b\sin c}.$$
The denominator is positive ([[cor-pi-is-the-first-positive-sine-zero]]). Whenever $z_S(a;b,c)\in[-1,1]$, define the **spherical comparison angle** by $\theta_S(a;b,c):=\arccos z_S(a;b,c)\in[0,\pi]$. No spherical angle is assigned by this definition when that validity condition fails. In either model the notation chooses the unique angle in $[0,\pi]$ having the indicated cosine.

**(2) Comparison angle of a metric hinge.** In a metric space $(X,d)$ ([[def-metric-space]]), let $p,x,y\in X$ with $x\ne p$ and $y\ne p$; $x=y$ is allowed. The **Euclidean comparison angle** at $p$ is
$$\widetilde\angle_p(x,y):=\theta_E\bigl(d(x,y);d(p,x),d(p,y)\bigr).$$
Its length triple meets (1): the metric triangle inequality gives $d(x,y)\le d(p,x)+d(p,y)$ and, applied with each of $x,y$ as the middle point, $|d(p,x)-d(p,y)|\le d(x,y)$.

**(3) Alexandrov upper angle.** Let $c:[0,L]\to X$ and $c':[0,L']\to X$ be unit-speed geodesic segments with $L,L'>0$ and $c(0)=c'(0)$ ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]). For $\varepsilon>0$ set
$$H(\varepsilon):=\sup\bigl\{\widetilde\angle_{c(0)}(c(s),c'(t)):0<s\le\min(\varepsilon,L),\ 0<t\le\min(\varepsilon,L')\bigr\},$$
and define their **Alexandrov upper angle** by
$$\angle(c,c'):=\inf_{\varepsilon>0}H(\varepsilon).$$
Each set in the supremum is nonempty and contained in $[0,\pi]$, so its supremum exists and also lies in $[0,\pi]$ ([[def-upper-bound]], [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]). The set of these suprema is likewise nonempty and bounded; its infimum exists by applying the same least-upper-bound property to its negatives. Thus $\angle(c,c')\in[0,\pi]$ is well defined. This is the two-variable upper-limit convention, without asserting existence of an ordinary limit, monotonicity of the comparison angles in $s,t$, invariance under reparametrization, or a CAT inequality.

**(4) Triangle-angle conventions.** In a geodesic triangle with distinct vertices and chosen sides ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]), the angle at a vertex means (3) for the unit-speed parametrizations of the two sides starting there. For a model triangle in $\mathbb M^2_\kappa$, $\kappa\in\{0,1\}$, with distinct vertices, the model angle at a vertex is defined by (1) from its two adjacent side lengths and opposite side length. In the spherical case the side lengths must be in $(0,\pi)$ and the validity condition in (1) must hold. Model angles are therefore side-length comparison angles; the identification with geometric angles, and any further relations among upper angles, require their own arguments.
items.strategy: Define length-triple comparison angles with the exact admissible domains; justify the Euclidean cosine range by both squared triangle inequalities and the upper-angle infimum/supremum by the published real least-upper-bound property. Preserve the existing upper-angle and model-angle conventions without asserting their further relations.

items.title: Comparison triangles in the Euclidean plane and the round sphere, model spaces, and CAT(0) and CAT(1) consequences
items.statement:
**(i) Euclidean comparison.** For all reals $a,b,c\ge0$ with $a\le b+c$, $b\le c+a$, $c\le a+b$ there are $\bar p,\bar q,\bar r\in\mathbb E^2$ with the three prescribed distances, and any two such triangles are related by an isometry of $\mathbb E^2$ ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]). Consequently every geodesic triangle in every metric space has a comparison triangle in $\mathbb E^2$, and the plane is CAT(0): for a triangle in $\mathbb E^2$ the comparison triangle is congruent to it and the defining inequality is an equality.

**(ii) The round sphere.** For $n\ge2$ the function $d_S(x,y)=\arccos(x\cdot y)$ is a metric on $S^{n-1}\subset\mathbb R^n$; $(S^{n-1},d_S)$ is a geodesic space whose geodesic segments are the minimal great-circle arcs; two points at distance $<\pi$ are joined by a unique geodesic segment; and every closed ball of radius $<\pi/2$ is convex ([[def-metric-ball]]). For every triple of side lengths with perimeter $<2\pi$ satisfying the triangle inequalities there is a comparison triangle in $S^2$, unique up to an isometry of $S^2$. Hence $S^2$ is CAT(1), the CAT(1) inequality for a triangle in $S^2$ of perimeter $<2\pi$ being an equality.

**(iii) Spherical cosine rule and midpoint identity.** For $A,B,C\in S^2$ with $a=d_S(B,C),b=d_S(C,A)\in(0,\pi)$, $c=d_S(A,B)<\pi$ and vertex angle $\gamma$ at $C$, $\cos c=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b\cos\gamma$. If $c<\pi$, $a$ is the midpoint of a geodesic $[y,z]$ of length $c$ and $x\in S^2$, then $$\cos d_S(x,a)=\frac{\cos d_S(x,y)+\cos d_S(x,z)}{2\cos(c/2)},\qquad \cos(c/2)>0.$$

**(iv) Consequences of CAT(0).** Let $X$ be CAT(0). Then: (a) geodesic segments between two points are unique and vary continuously with their endpoints ([[def-geodesic-and-geodesic-metric-space]]); (b) if $\gamma,\delta$ are geodesics with a common initial point and proportional parametrizations, then $d(\gamma(t),\delta(t))\le(1-t)d(\gamma(0),\delta(0))+t\,d(\gamma(1),\delta(1))$ for $t\in[0,1]$; (c) (hinged criterion) for a geodesic triangle with vertices $z,x,y$ and the point $p_t$ on $[x,y]$ at distance $t\,d(x,y)$ from $x$, the CAT(0) inequality $d(z,p_t)\le d_2(\bar z,\bar p_t)$ holds if and only if $$d(z,p_t)^2\le(1-t)d(z,x)^2+t\,d(z,y)^2-t(1-t)d(x,y)^2,$$ the right-hand side being the squared Euclidean comparison distance; consequently a geodesic space is CAT(0) if and only if for every geodesic triangle and every point $x$ on a side the comparison inequality $d(p,x)\le d_2(\bar p,\bar x)$ with the opposite vertex $p$ holds; (d) for every pair $y,y'$, every midpoint $m$ of a geodesic segment $[y,y']$ and every $z$, $d(z,m)^2\le\tfrac12(d(z,y)^2+d(z,y')^2)-\tfrac14 d(y,y')^2$.

**(v) CAT(1) short-geodesic estimates.** Let $X$ be CAT(1), $p\in X$, $0<r<\pi/2$ and $x,y,z\in B(p,r)$. Then $B(p,r)$ is convex, $[y,z]$ is unique with midpoint $a$, and, **whenever the CAT(1) test is admissible, i.e. $d(x,y)+d(y,z)+d(z,x)<2\pi$**, $$\cos d(x,a)\ge\frac{\cos d(x,y)+\cos d(x,z)}{2\cos(d(y,z)/2)},$$ where $d(y,z)\le2r<\pi$ makes the denominator positive. The admissibility bound is a hypothesis and not a consequence of $r<\pi/2$: a triple in such a ball has perimeter $<6r$ only, and the CAT(1) inequality is stated for triangles of perimeter $<2\pi$.

**(vi) The round circle.** For every $\ell>0$, $d_\ell$ is a metric on $S^1_\ell$ ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]); $(S^1_\ell,d_\ell)$ is a compact complete geodesic space locally isometric to $\mathbb R$, contains an isometrically embedded circle of length $\ell$, and is CAT(1) if and only if $\ell\ge2\pi$. For $\ell<2\pi$ the points $0,\ell/3,2\ell/3$ form a triangle of perimeter $\ell<2\pi$ whose side midpoint is at distance $\ell/2$ from the opposite vertex, which exceeds the distance in the spherical comparison triangle; for $\ell\ge2\pi$ every triangle of perimeter $<2\pi$ lies in an arc of length $<\pi$, hence is degenerate and realizes its comparison triangle isometrically.
items.strategy:
1.1 The series of [[def-sine-and-cosine-by-power-series]] contain only even powers of $t$ in $\cos t$ and only odd powers in $\sin t$, so $\cos(-t)=\cos t$, $\sin(-t)=-\sin t$, $\cos0=1$ and $\sin0=0$; replacing $y$ by $-y$ in [F4] therefore gives $\cos(x-y)=\cos x\cos y+\sin x\sin y$ and $\sin(x-y)=\sin x\cos y-\cos x\sin y$, and the case $x=y=t$ of the cosine subtraction formula gives the Pythagorean identity $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=\cos0=1$, whence $\cos2t=2\cos^2t-1$. Since $\sin\pi=0$ by [F5], $\cos^2\pi=1$; $\cos$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ by [F3] with $\cos0=1$, so $\cos\pi<1$ and hence $\cos\pi=-1$; then $0=\cos\pi+1=2\cos^2(\pi/2)$ gives $\cos(\pi/2)=0$, and strict decrease gives $\cos t>0$ for $0\le t<\pi/2$. [F3, F4, F5, algebra]

1.2 Let $a,b,c>0$ satisfy the three triangle inequalities and put $t:=(b^2+c^2-a^2)/(2b)$ and $s:=\sqrt{c^2-t^2}$, which is real because $c^2-t^2=\frac{(a+b+c)(b+c-a)(a+c-b)(a+b-c)}{4b^2}\ge0$; set $\bar p:=(0,0)$, $\bar r:=(b,0)$ and $\bar q:=(t,s)$ in $\mathbb R^2$. Then $d_2(\bar p,\bar r)=b$, $d_2(\bar p,\bar q)^2=t^2+s^2=c^2$ and $d_2(\bar r,\bar q)^2=(t-b)^2+s^2=t^2-2bt+b^2+s^2=c^2+b^2-2bt=a^2$, so the three prescribed distances are realised. This construction includes every positive degenerate triple because then $s=0$. If $b=0$, the inequalities force $a=c$, and $\bar p=\bar r=(0,0)$, $\bar q=(c,0)$ realise the triple; the other zero-side cases follow by relabeling. [F7, algebra]

1.3 For $x,y\in S^{n-1}$ the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality [F6] gives $|x\cdot y|\le1$, so $d_S(x,y)=\arccos(x\cdot y)$ is defined by [F2]; symmetry is $x\cdot y=y\cdot x$, separation at $x=y$ is $\arccos1=0$, and if $d_S(x,y)=0$ then $x\cdot y=1$, so $x,y$ are linearly dependent by the equality case of [F6]; as unit vectors they satisfy $y=\pm x$, and $x\cdot y=1$ excludes $y=-x$, so $x=y$. [F2, F6, F8, algebra]

1.4 Let $A,B,C\in S^{n-1}$ with $a:=d_S(B,C)$ and $b:=d_S(C,A)$ both in $(0,\pi)$, and let $c:=d_S(A,B)$, $u:=\bigl(B-(B\cdot C)C\bigr)/|B-(B\cdot C)C|$ and $v:=\bigl(A-(A\cdot C)C\bigr)/|A-(A\cdot C)C|$. Here $B\cdot C=\cos a$ and $A\cdot C=\cos b$ by [F2], so $|B-(B\cdot C)C|^2=1-\cos^2a=\sin^2a>0$ and likewise $|A-(A\cdot C)C|^2=\sin^2b>0$, using $\sin a>0$ and $\sin b>0$ from [F5]; hence $B=(\cos a)C+(\sin a)u$ and $A=(\cos b)C+(\sin b)v$ with $u,v$ unit vectors orthogonal to $C$. Expanding gives the spherical cosine rule $\cos c=A\cdot B=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b\,(u\cdot v)$, and $\cos\gamma:=u\cdot v\in[-1,1]$ by [F6] defines the vertex angle $\gamma\in[0,\pi]$ at $C$. [F2, F5, F6, algebra]

1.5 Let $X$ be a geodesic space with a geodesic triangle $z,x,y$ and $p_t$ on $[x,y]$ at distance $t\,d(x,y)$ from $x$; in the Euclidean comparison triangle $\bar p_t=(1-t)\bar x+t\bar y$, so the identity $|\bar z-\bar p_t|^2=(1-t)|\bar z-\bar x|^2+t|\bar z-\bar y|^2-t(1-t)|\bar x-\bar y|^2$ holds by expansion, and substituting the comparison distances shows that $d(z,p_t)\le d_2(\bar z,\bar p_t)$ is equivalent to its squared form, both sides being nonnegative. [F1, algebra]

1.6 On $S^1_\ell=\mathbb R/\ell\mathbb Z$ the minimum defining $d_\ell$ exists: for $\delta=x-y$, choose $N>2|\delta|/\ell$ by [F13]; when $|k|>N$, $|\delta+k\ell|\ge|k|\ell-|\delta|>|\delta|$, so a minimum occurs among the finitely many integers $|k|\le N$. Changing representatives just shifts these integers. Thus $d_\ell$ is well defined and symmetric and vanishes exactly on the diagonal, and $d_\ell(x,z)=\min_k|x-z+k\ell|\le\min_k|x-y+k\ell|+\min_j|y-z+j\ell|=d_\ell(x,y)+d_\ell(y,z)$ by choosing minimising integers; hence $d_\ell$ is a metric. The map $t\mapsto t+\ell\mathbb Z$ from $[0,\ell]$ onto $S^1_\ell$ is surjective: a finite integer bound from [F13] permits subtracting an integer multiple of $\ell$ to place each real representative in $[0,\ell)$ and satisfies $d_\ell(s,t)=\min(|s-t|,\ell-|s-t|)$ for $s,t\in[0,\ell]$, so it is continuous and sends the compact interval onto $S^1_\ell$, which is therefore compact, complete by [F11] and geodesic (the shorter interval between two parameters is mapped isometrically), and each point has a ball of radius $r<\ell/4$ isometric to an interval of $\mathbb R$, since differences between lifts in that ball are $<\ell/2$. A minimizing segment lifts successively through these interval charts, starting at any chosen lift; each chart restriction of its lift is affine of slope $+1$ or $-1$ in unit-speed parameters. Overlaps fix the same slope, so the lift is one straight interval. Therefore all minimizing segments are the shorter arcs, with two choices only at distance $\ell/2$; the identity map exhibits an isometrically embedded circle of length $\ell$ in the sense of [F9]. [F1, F9, F10, F11, F13, algebra]

2.1 Two triangles in $\mathbb R^2$ with the same three side lengths are related by an isometry: when all lengths are zero all vertices coincide, and a translation suffices; otherwise relabel so that the baseline has positive length. If $d_2(P,R)=b>0$, the map $\phi(x):=P+Bx$, with $B$ orthogonal sending $(1,0)$ to $(R-P)/b$, is an isometry of $\mathbb R^2$, and applying the coordinate computation of step 1.2 to $\phi^{-1}$ of a triangle shows that a point $Q$ at distance $c$ from $P$ and $a$ from $R$ has coordinates $(t,\pm s)$ with $t,s$ as in step 1.2; the two solutions differ by the reflection $(x_1,x_2)\mapsto(x_1,-x_2)$, so any two triangles with the prescribed side lengths are obtained from the normal form of step 1.2 by an isometry. [step 1.2, F9, algebra]

2.2 With the notation of step 1.4 and $a,b\in(0,\pi)$: if $a+b\le\pi$ then $\cos c\ge\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin b=\cos(a+b)$ by [F4] and $\sin a\sin b\ge0$ from [F5], and since $c\le\pi$ and $\cos$ strictly decreases on $[0,\pi]$ by [F3], $c\le a+b$; if $a+b>\pi$ then $c\le\pi<a+b$. If $a=0$ then $C=B$ and $c=b=a+b$; if $b=0$ similarly $c=a$. Hence $d_S$ satisfies the triangle inequality, and by step 1.3 it is a metric on $S^{n-1}$. [step 1.3, step 1.4, F1, F3, F4, F5]

2.3 Let $x,y\in S^{n-1}$ and $\theta:=d_S(x,y)\in(0,\pi]$; when $\theta<\pi$ put $\xi:=(y-(x\cdot y)x)/|y-(x\cdot y)x|$, so that $y=(\cos\theta)x+(\sin\theta)\xi$ with $\xi$ a unit vector orthogonal to $x$ by step 1.3 and [F2], and choose any unit $\xi\perp x$ when $\theta=\pi$. Then $c(t):=(\cos t)x+(\sin t)\xi$ satisfies $c(0)=x$, $c(\theta)=y$, and $c(t)\cdot c(t')=\cos(t-t')$ for $t,t'\in[0,\theta]$ with $|t-t'|\le\theta\le\pi$ by step 1.1, so $d_S(c(t),c(t'))=|t-t'|$ by [F2]; thus minimal great-circle arcs are geodesic segments in the sense of [F12]. [step 1.1, step 1.3, F2, F12, algebra]

2.4 Let $a,b,c\ge0$ satisfy the triangle inequalities with $a+b+c<2\pi$. Then $a,b,c<\pi$, since $a\ge\pi$ forces $a+b+c\ge2a\ge2\pi$. If $a,b,c>0$, put $\gamma:=\arccos\frac{\cos c-\cos a\cos b}{\sin a\sin b}$; the argument lies in $[-1,1]$ directly from the length hypotheses. Indeed $c\ge|a-b|$ gives $\cos c\le\cos(a-b)=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b$. If $a+b\le\pi$, then $c\le a+b$ gives $\cos c\ge\cos(a+b)$; if $a+b>\pi$, the perimeter bound gives $c<2\pi-a-b<\pi$, hence $\cos c>\cos(2\pi-a-b)=\cos(a+b)$. In both cases $\cos c\ge\cos a\cos b-\sin a\sin b$, proving the required range without presupposing a spherical realization, and the construction $C:=(1,0,0)$, $B:=(\cos a)C+(\sin a)(0,1,0)$, $A:=(\cos b)C+(\sin b)\bigl(\cos\gamma\,(0,1,0)+\sin\gamma\,(0,0,1)\bigr)$ uses $\cos^2t+\sin^2t=1$ (step 1.1) to give unit vectors with $B\cdot C=\cos a$, $A\cdot C=\cos b$ and $A\cdot B=\cos a\cos b+\sin a\sin b\cos\gamma=\cos c$; if one of $a,b,c$ vanishes, say $a=0$, then $b=c$ and $C:=(1,0,0)$, $B:=C$, $A:=(\cos b)C+(\sin b)(0,1,0)$ realise the triple. Any two triples of unit vectors with equal pairwise inner products have spans related by a well-defined inner-product-preserving linear map, extended to an orthogonal map of $\mathbb R^3$ along orthonormal bases of the orthocomplements; so the comparison triangle is unique up to an isometry of $S^2$ by [F9]. A triangle in $S^2$ of perimeter $<2\pi$ is a comparison triangle for itself, so the CAT(1) inequality holds with equality for it and $S^2$ is CAT(1). [step 1.1, step 1.4, F1, F2, F6, F9]

2.5 Let $X$ be CAT(0) and let $\gamma,\delta$ be geodesic segments from $x$ to $y$ of length $L=d(x,y)$; the geodesic triangle with sides $\gamma,\delta$ and the degenerate third side has side lengths $L,L,0$, and its comparison triangle in $\mathbb E^2$ is degenerate with the comparison points of $\gamma(t)$ and $\delta(t)$ coinciding, both being at distance $t$ from the comparison vertex $\bar x$ along the same comparison side; hence $d(\gamma(t),\delta(t))\le d_2(\bar\gamma(t),\bar\delta(t))=0$ by the CAT(0) inequality, so $\gamma=\delta$ and geodesic segments are unique. [step 1.2, F1, F12]

3.1 A geodesic triangle in a metric space has side lengths obeying the triangle inequalities, because the metric satisfies (M3) of [[def-metric-space]]; in $\mathbb E^2$ every geodesic side is a straight segment: equality $|x-w|+|w-y|=|x-y|$ along a minimizing segment forces the two displacement vectors to be nonnegative multiples by the equality case of [F6], and their lengths fix $w$. By steps 1.2 and 2.1 every metric triangle therefore has a comparison triangle in $\mathbb E^2$, unique up to isometry, and if the triangle itself lies in $\mathbb E^2$ then it is a comparison triangle for itself by step 2.1, so the CAT(0) inequality is an equality for it and $\mathbb E^2$ is CAT(0). [step 1.2, step 2.1, F1, F6, F12]

3.2 Let $x,y\in S^{n-1}$, $\theta:=d_S(x,y)\in(0,\pi)$, and let $z\in S^{n-1}$ satisfy $d_S(x,z)+d_S(z,y)=\theta$; write $\alpha:=d_S(x,z)$ and $\beta:=d_S(z,y)$, so $\theta=\alpha+\beta$. The Gram matrix of $x,y,z$ has entries $x\cdot x=y\cdot y=z\cdot z=1$, $x\cdot y=\cos\theta$, $x\cdot z=\cos\alpha$, $y\cdot z=\cos\beta$, and is positive semidefinite because $v^{T}Gv=|\sum_iv_iu_i|^2\ge0$; by step 1.1, $\cos\theta=\cos(\alpha+\beta)=\cos\alpha\cos\beta-\sin\alpha\sin\beta$, so its determinant is $1+2\cos\alpha\cos\beta\cos\theta-\cos^2\alpha-\cos^2\beta-\cos^2\theta=\sin^2\alpha\sin^2\beta-(\cos\theta-\cos\alpha\cos\beta)^2=0$, the bracket being $\sin\alpha\sin\beta$. Hence $x,y,z$ are linearly dependent; since $\theta\in(0,\pi)$ makes $x,y$ independent, $z$ lies in the plane $P:=\mathrm{span}\{x,y\}$. Parametrise the unit circle of $P$ by $c(s)=(\cos s)x+(\sin s)\xi$ with $\xi$ as in step 2.3, so that $y=c(\theta)$; a unit vector of $P$ with $x\cdot z=\cos\alpha$ is $c(\alpha)$ or $c(-\alpha)$, and if $z=c(-\alpha)$ with $\alpha>0$ then $z\cdot y=c(-\alpha)\cdot c(\theta)=\cos(\theta+\alpha)\ne\cos(\theta-\alpha)=\cos\beta$ by steps 1.1 and 1.4, since equality would force $\sin\theta\sin\alpha=0$; so $z=c(\alpha)$, a point of the minimal arc from $x$ to $y$. [step 1.1, step 1.4, step 2.3, F2, F4, F6, algebra]

3.3 Let $p\in S^{n-1}$, $0<r<\pi/2$ and $x,y\in\bar B(p,r)$; if $x=y$ there is nothing to prove, so assume $x\ne y$ and put $\theta:=d_S(x,y)\in(0,\pi]$. If $\theta=\pi$ then $y=-x$ by [F2], so $p\cdot y=-p\cdot x\le-\cos r$ while $p\cdot y=\cos d_S(p,y)\ge\cos r$, a contradiction since $\cos r>0$; hence $\theta<\pi$. For $0\le t\le\theta$ the point $c(t)=\frac{\sin(\theta-t)}{\sin\theta}x+\frac{\sin t}{\sin\theta}y$ of the arc of step 2.3 has nonnegative coefficients by [F5], whose sum is $\cos(t-\theta/2)/\cos(\theta/2)\ge1$ by the addition formulas and decreasing cosine, so $p\cdot c(t)\ge\min(p\cdot x,p\cdot y)\ge\cos r>0$ and therefore $d_S(p,c(t))\le r$ by [F2] and [F3]; hence $\bar B(p,r)$ is convex. [step 2.3, F2, F3, F5, algebra]

3.4 Let $\gamma,\delta$ be geodesics with common initial point $x=\gamma(0)=\delta(0)$ and proportional parametrisations on $[0,1]$; if $\gamma(1)=\delta(1)$ the claim follows from step 2.5, so let $y:=\gamma(1)$, $z:=\delta(1)$ and consider the geodesic triangle $x,y,z$. In its Euclidean comparison triangle the points $\bar\gamma(t)$ and $\bar\delta(t)$ are at distance $t\,d(y,z)$ for every $t\in[0,1]$, by similarity; the CAT(0) inequality applied to the pair $\gamma(t),\delta(t)$ gives $d(\gamma(t),\delta(t))\le t\,d(y,z)=(1-t)d(\gamma(0),\delta(0))+t\,d(\gamma(1),\delta(1))$ since $\gamma(0)=\delta(0)$. [step 2.5, F1, algebra]

3.5 Let $X$ be a geodesic space in which the CAT(0) inequality holds for every geodesic triangle and every pair consisting of a vertex and a point of the opposite side. Then it holds for all pairs. If $x,y$ lie on one side the comparison preserves distances along that side; if one of $x,y$ is a vertex of the triangle, the claim is either the hypothesis (when the other point lies on the opposite side) or the equality of a side length with its comparison length (when the other point is a vertex or lies on an adjacent side and equals the shared vertex); and degenerate triangles, where some side has length $0$, reduce to these cases. It remains to treat a triangle with sides $[p,q],[q,r],[r,p]$, points $x\in[p,q]$ and $y\in[p,r]$ with $x\ne p\ne y$, $x\ne q$ and $y\ne r$, comparison triangle $(\bar p,\bar q,\bar r)$, comparison points $\bar x\in[\bar p,\bar q]$ and $\bar y\in[\bar p,\bar r]$, and the positive numbers $a:=d(p,x)$, $b:=d(p,y)$; write $\hat d:=d(x,y)$ and let $\hat\alpha$ be the vertex angle at the point corresponding to $p$ in the comparison triangle of $(p,x,y)$, so that $\hat d^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos\hat\alpha$. Apply the hypothesis to the geodesic triangle $(p,x,r)$ with vertex $x$ and the point $y$ of the opposite side $[p,r]$: if $(\hat p',\hat x',\hat r')$ is the comparison triangle of $(p,x,r)$ and $\hat y'\in[\hat p',\hat r']$ is the comparison point of $y$, then $\hat d\le D:=d_2(\hat x',\hat y')$. The triangles $(\hat p',\hat x',\hat y')$ and the comparison triangle of $(p,x,y)$ have two sides in common, of lengths $a$ and $b$, and opposite sides $D\ge\hat d$, so the angle at $\hat p'$ of the former is at least $\hat\alpha$: for fixed $a,b>0$ the quantity $(a^2+b^2-s^2)/(2ab)$ is strictly decreasing in $s$ and $\cos$ is strictly decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ (F3), so the included angle is increasing in the opposite side. As $\hat y'$ lies on the side $[\hat p',\hat r']$, that angle is exactly the vertex angle $\hat\alpha'$ of the comparison triangle of $(p,x,r)$ at $\hat p'$, so $\hat\alpha'\ge\hat\alpha$. Apply the hypothesis again, to $(p,q,r)$ with vertex $r$ and the point $x$ of the opposite side $[p,q]$: $d(r,x)\le d_2(\bar r,\bar x)$, so the triangles $(\hat p',\hat x',\hat r')$ and $(\bar p,\bar x,\bar r)$ have two sides in common, of lengths $a$ and $d(p,r)$, and opposite sides $d(x,r)\le d_2(\bar x,\bar r)$; the same monotonicity of the included angle gives $\hat\alpha'\le\bar\alpha$, the vertex angle of $(\bar p,\bar q,\bar r)$ at $\bar p$, and $\bar x\in[\bar p,\bar q]$ with $\bar x\ne\bar p$ makes the ray from $\bar p$ to $\bar x$ the ray to $\bar q$, so this angle is exactly the vertex angle of $(\bar p,\bar x,\bar r)$ at $\bar p$. Hence $\hat\alpha\le\bar\alpha$, and the two laws of cosines $d(x,y)^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos\hat\alpha$ and $d_2(\bar x,\bar y)^2=a^2+b^2-2ab\cos\bar\alpha$ give $d(x,y)\le d_2(\bar x,\bar y)$ because $\cos$ is decreasing on $[0,\pi]$ (F3). Thus a geodesic space is CAT(0) if and only if every vertex-opposite-side comparison holds. [step 1.5, step 2.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.6 The case $t=1/2$ of the squared form in step 1.5, with $m:=p_{1/2}$ a midpoint of $[y,y']:=[x,y]$ and $z$ the opposite vertex, gives $d(z,m)^2\le\tfrac12 d(z,y)^2+\tfrac12 d(z,y')^2-\tfrac14 d(y,y')^2$, which is (d) since midpoints are unique by step 2.5. [step 1.5, step 2.5]

3.7 Let $\ell\ge2\pi$ and let $x,y,z\in S^1_\ell$ be the vertices of a triangle of perimeter $p<2\pi$, so that all three sides are $<\pi$; if vertices repeat, the two nonzero sides coincide by the circle interval charts: a minimizing circle path of length $<\ell/2$ has a lift with one fixed direction in the overlapping interval charts, hence is the shorter arc. Such triangles realize a degenerate comparison. For three distinct vertices write their cyclic gaps as $g_1,g_2,g_3>0$. If all $g_i\le\ell/2$ then the three pairwise distances are $g_1,g_2,g_3$ and $p=\ell\ge2\pi$, contrary to hypothesis; so some $g_3>\ell/2$, the complementary arc of length $s:=\ell-g_3$ contains all three points, and the two adjacent distances are $g_1,g_2$ while the third is $g_1+g_2=s$, so $p=2s<2\pi$ and $s<\pi$. Thus the triangle is degenerate and isometric, side by side, to a configuration on an arc of length $s$; placing three points of a great arc of $S^2$ of the same length $s<\pi$ realises the same three side lengths, so by uniqueness of comparison triangles in step 2.4 the comparison triangle is isometric to the triangle and the CAT(1) inequality holds with equality; hence $S^1_\ell$ is CAT(1) for $\ell\ge2\pi$. [step 2.4, F1, algebra]

4.1 Geodesic segments in a CAT(0) space vary continuously with their endpoints. Let $\gamma$ be the geodesic from $x$ to $y$ and $\gamma'$ the geodesic from $x'$ to $y'$, let $t\in[0,1]$, and let $\delta$ be the geodesic from $x$ to $y'$, so that $\gamma,\delta$ are geodesics from the common initial point $x$ with proportional parametrizations. Step 3.4 gives $d(\gamma(t),\delta(t))\le(1-t)d(\gamma(0),\delta(0))+t\,d(\gamma(1),\delta(1))=t\,d(y,y')$, and step 3.4 applied to the reversed geodesics $\bar\delta(s)=\delta(1-s)$ from $y'$ to $x$ and $\bar\gamma'(s)=\gamma'(1-s)$ from $y'$ to $x'$, which again have a common initial point and proportional parametrizations, gives $d(\delta(t),\gamma'(t))=d(\bar\delta(1-t),\bar\gamma'(1-t))\le(1-t)\,d(x,x')$. Hence $d(\gamma(t),\gamma'(t))\le(1-t)\,d(x,x')+t\,d(y,y')$ for every $t$, which tends to $0$ uniformly in $t$ as $x'\to x$ and $y'\to y$; since the geodesic segments are unique by step 2.5, they vary continuously with their endpoints as asserted in (iv)(a). [step 2.5, step 3.4, F1]


4.2 Let $\gamma:[0,\theta]\to S^{n-1}$ be a geodesic from $x$ to $y$ with $\theta<\pi$. If $\theta=0$ it is constant. Otherwise $d_S(x,\gamma(t))+d_S(\gamma(t),y)=\theta$, so step 3.2 puts $\gamma(t)$ on the unique minimal arc at position $t$, and step 2.3 identifies its parametrization. If $\theta=\pi$, choose $z=\gamma(\pi/2)$, perpendicular to $x$. Each half has length $\pi/2$ and is the unique short arc just proved; because $y=-x$, both halves lie in the plane spanned by $x,z$ and form one semicircle. This proves the claimed classification of all spherical geodesics. [step 2.3, step 3.2, F2, F12, algebra]

4.3 Let $X$ be CAT(1), $p\in X$, $0<r<\pi/2$ and $y,z\in B(p,r)$. Since $d(y,z)<2r<\pi$, segments exist. Two competing segments give a triangle with repeated vertex and perimeter $2d(y,z)<2\pi$; its comparison sides coincide, so CAT(1) forces equal-parameter points to coincide. Thus $[y,z]$ is unique. Choose $r'$ with $\max\{d(p,y),d(p,z)\}<r'<r$. The triangle $p,y,z$ has perimeter $<4r'<2\pi$. Its comparison side lies in the convex spherical ball $\bar B(\bar p,r')$ by step 3.3, so CAT(1) gives $d(p,w)\le r'<r$ for every $w\in[y,z]$. Hence $B(p,r)$ is convex, and the same argument with non-strict endpoint bounds proves convexity of closed balls of radius $<\pi/2$. [step 2.4, step 3.3, F1, F12, choose]

5.1 Let $y,z\in S^2$ with $c:=d_S(y,z)<\pi$ and $x\in S^2$; put $a:=(y+z)/|y+z|$, a unit vector because $y\ne-z$. Then $y\cdot a=z\cdot a=(1+\cos c)/|y+z|>0$, since $\cos c>-1=\cos\pi$ by step 1.1 and [F3], so $s:=d_S(y,a)=d_S(z,a)$ by [F2] and $\cos s>0$. Since $|y+z|^2=2+2\cos c$ (step 1.1) and $s=\arccos(y\cdot a)$, we get $\cos^2s=(1+\cos c)/2$, hence $\cos c=2\cos^2s-1=\cos2s$ by step 1.1; as $c,2s\in[0,\pi]$ and $\cos$ is injective there by [F3], $c=2s$ and $\cos(c/2)=\cos s>0$. Finally $\cos d_S(x,a)=x\cdot a=\frac{x\cdot y+x\cdot z}{|y+z|}=\frac{\cos d_S(x,y)+\cos d_S(x,z)}{2\cos(c/2)}$, using $|y+z|=2\cos(c/2)$. [step 1.1, step 4.2, F2, F3, algebra]

6.1 Let $X$ be CAT(1), $p\in X$, $0<r<\pi/2$ and $x,y,z\in B(p,r)$ with $d(x,y)+d(y,z)+d(z,x)<2\pi$; the sides are $<2r<\pi$, so $[y,z]$ is unique with midpoint $a$ by step 4.3 and the CAT(1) inequality applied to the pair $(x,a)$ of the triangle $x,y,z$ gives $d(x,a)\le d_S(\bar x,\bar a)$, where $\bar a$ is the midpoint of the comparison side $[\bar y,\bar z]$ of length $d(y,z)$. Step 5.1 applied in $S^2$ to $\bar x,\bar y,\bar z$ gives $\cos d_S(\bar x,\bar a)=\frac{\cos d_S(\bar x,\bar y)+\cos d_S(\bar x,\bar z)}{2\cos(d(y,z)/2)}$, and since $d(x,a)\le d_S(\bar x,\bar a)\le\pi$ and $\cos$ strictly decreases on $[0,\pi]$ by [F3], $\cos d(x,a)\ge\cos d_S(\bar x,\bar a)=\frac{\cos d(x,y)+\cos d(x,z)}{2\cos(d(y,z)/2)}$, the denominator being positive by step 5.1. [step 4.3, step 5.1, F1, F3]

6.2 Let $\ell<2\pi$ and let $x:=0$, $y:=\ell/3$, $z:=2\ell/3$ in $S^1_\ell$; the three pairwise distances are $\ell/3<\pi$, so the triangle has perimeter $\ell<2\pi$; let $a:=\ell/6$ be the midpoint of $[x,y]$, so $d_\ell(a,z)=\min\{\ell/2,\ell/2\}=\ell/2$. In the comparison triangle in $S^2$, whose sides all have length $\ell/3$, the midpoint $\bar a$ of a side satisfies $\cos d_S(\bar a,\bar z)=\frac{\cos(\ell/3)}{\cos(\ell/6)}$ by step 5.1, with $\cos(\ell/6)>0$ by step 1.1 since $\ell/6<\pi/3<\pi/2$; and step 1.1 gives $\cos(\ell/6)\cos(\ell/2)=\tfrac12\cos(2\ell/3)+\tfrac12\cos(\ell/3)<\tfrac12\cos(\ell/3)+\tfrac12\cos(\ell/3)=\cos(\ell/3)$, because $\cos(2\ell/3)-\cos(\ell/3)=-2\sin(\ell/2)\sin(\ell/6)<0$ by the addition formulas and [F5]. Dividing by $\cos(\ell/6)>0$ gives $\cos(\ell/2)<\frac{\cos(\ell/3)}{\cos(\ell/6)}=\cos d_S(\bar a,\bar z)$, that is $d_S(\bar a,\bar z)<\ell/2=d_\ell(a,z)$; the CAT(1) inequality fails at the pair $(a,z)$ by step 1.4 and [F3]. [step 1.1, step 1.4, step 5.1, F1, F3, algebra]

7.1 Combining steps 3.7 and 6.2 with the metric, compactness, completeness and local flatness of step 1.6 proves every assertion of (vi), and steps 3.1, 4.2, 4.3, 3.4, 3.5, 3.6, 4.1 and 6.1 prove (i) to (v). [step 1.6, step 3.1, step 3.4, step 3.5, step 3.6, step 3.7, step 4.1, step 4.2, step 4.3, step 6.1, step 6.2] ∎

items.title: Alexandrov comparison: straightening a hinge, gluing comparison triangles, and patchwork
items.statement:
**(i) Alexandrov's Lemma.** Let $\kappa\in\{0,1\}$, let $\mathbb M^2_\kappa$ be $\mathbb E^2$ for $\kappa=0$ and $S^2$ for $\kappa=1$, and let $A,B,B',C$ be four distinct points of $\mathbb M^2_\kappa$; if $\kappa=1$ assume $d(C,B)+d(C,B')+d(A,B)+d(A,B')<2\pi$. Suppose $B$ and $B'$ lie on opposite sides of the geodesic line through $A$ and $C$. Let $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ and $\alpha',\beta',\gamma'$ be the angles of the triangles $\Delta(A,B,C)$ and $\Delta(A,B',C)$ at $A,B,C$ and $A,B',C$. If $\gamma+\gamma'\ge\pi$, then

(1) $d(B,C)+d(B',C)\le d(B,A)+d(B',A)$;

(2) if $\Delta''$ is a triangle with vertices $\bar A,\bar B,\bar B'$ such that $d(\bar A,\bar B)=d(A,B)$, $d(\bar A,\bar B')=d(A,B')$ and $d(\bar B,\bar B')=d(B,C)+d(C,B')$, and $\bar C\in[\bar B,\bar B']$ satisfies $d(\bar B,\bar C)=d(B,C)$, then the angle $\bar\alpha$ of $\Delta''$ at $\bar A$, the angle $\bar\beta'$ of $\Delta''$ at $\bar B'$ and the distance $d(\bar A,\bar C)$ satisfy $\bar\alpha\ge\alpha+\alpha'$, $\bar\beta'\ge\beta'$ and $d(\bar A,\bar C)\ge d(A,C)$; equality in any one of the three assertions implies the others and holds if and only if $\gamma+\gamma'=\pi$.

**(ii) Gluing Lemma for triangles.** Let $X$ be a metric space in which every pair of points at distance $<D_\kappa$ is joined by a geodesic, and let $\Delta=([q_0,q_1],[q_1,p],[p,q_0])$ be a geodesic triangle in $X$ of perimeter $<2D_\kappa$ with distinct vertices. Let $r\in[q_0,q_1]$ with $r\ne p$, let $[p,r]$ be a geodesic, and put $\Delta_1=([q_0,r],[r,p],[p,q_0])$ and $\Delta_2=([p,r],[r,q_1],[q_1,p])$. If for $i=1,2$ every defined vertex angle of a comparison triangle $\bar\Delta_i$ in $\mathbb M^2_\kappa$ is no smaller than the corresponding angle of $\Delta_i$, then the same is true for the angles of any comparison triangle for $\Delta$ ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]).

**(iii) Patchwork.** Let $X$ be a metric space of curvature $\le\kappa$, let $p,q_0,q_1\in X$ with $q_0\ne q_1$, $p\notin[q_0,q_1]$, and $d(p,q_0)+d(p,q_1)+d(q_0,q_1)<2D_\kappa$, let $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$ be a geodesic from $q_0$ to $q_1$, and let $c_s:[0,1]\to X$, $s\in[0,1]$, be geodesics from $p$ to $\gamma(s)$ depending continuously on $s$ with $c_0=[p,q_0]$ and $c_1=[p,q_1]$. Then the vertex angles of the triangle $\Delta=([q_0,q_1],[q_1,p],[p,q_0])$ are no greater than the corresponding angles of any comparison triangle in $\mathbb M^2_\kappa$. The same conclusion holds for a finite subdivision obtained by successive applications of (ii), provided each intermediate union is a geodesic triangle of perimeter $<2D_\kappa$ and its common-side splitting point lies on the opposite geodesic side.

**(iv) Upper-angle facts.** For nonconstant geodesic segments with a common initial point, restricting either segment to any nonzero initial subsegment leaves their Alexandrov upper angle unchanged. The two opposite directions at an interior point of a geodesic have upper angle $\pi$. For any three nonconstant geodesic segments $a,b,c$ with the same initial point, their upper angles satisfy $\angle(a,c)\le\angle(a,b)+\angle(b,c)$.
items.strategy:
1.1 Spherical size and orientation. The model comparison angles agree with geometric angles: on the sphere, the unit tangent towards $V$ at $U$ is $(V-(U\cdot V)U)/\sin d(U,V)$, whose dot product with the analogous tangent towards $W$ is exactly the cosine formula in [F2]; the Euclidean assertion is the corresponding dot-product formula. Write $u=d(C,B)$, $y=d(C,B')$, $p=d(A,B)$, $q=d(A,B')$, $x=d(A,C)$ and $L=u+y+p+q$. For $\kappa=1$, $L<2\pi$ gives $x<\pi$, since $2x\le(u+p)+(y+q)=L$; every boundary edge is also $<\pi$, since its complementary path has length at least that edge. The polygonal loop $A,B,C,B',A$ lies in an open hemisphere: take points $P,Q$ dividing its arclength into halves of length $L/2$; every point $Z$ on either half satisfies $d(P,Z)+d(Q,Z)\le L/2<\pi$, hence $(P+Q)\cdot Z=\cos d(P,Z)+\cos d(Q,Z)>0$. In that hemisphere the projection $Z\mapsto Z/(h\cdot Z)$, with $h=(P+Q)/\|P+Q\|$, maps minor great-circle arcs to straight segments and preserves the side of each line and whether an interior angle is reflex. Because $B,B'$ are on opposite sides of $AC$, the projected quadrilateral is simple. Its angles at $B,B'$ are convex, and its angle at $C$ is reflex or straight because $\gamma+\gamma'\ge\pi$. Triangulating along $AC$ shows that its angle at $A$ is convex and that $C$ lies in the closed triangle $ABB'$; the same conclusions hold before projection. Thus $\alpha+\alpha'\le\pi$. Moreover $u+y<\pi$: otherwise $p+q<\pi$, so $(B+B')\cdot A=\cos p+\cos q>0$, and $(B+B')\cdot B=(B+B')\cdot B'=1+B\cdot B'>0$ (the original open hemisphere excludes antipodal $B,B'$). A hemisphere contains the minor geodesic segments joining its points, since their unit vectors are normalized positive linear combinations; hence the hemisphere with pole $B+B'$ contains the spherical triangle $ABB'$ and $C$, giving $\cos u+\cos y>0$, equivalently $u+y<\pi$, a contradiction. In the Euclidean case the same planar quadrilateral argument gives $\alpha+\alpha'\le\pi$, and there is no size restriction. [F1, F2, F4, algebra, given]

1.2 A monotonicity lemma for a marked point. Let $V,W,U$ be a triangle in $\mathbb M^2_\kappa$ with $|VW|=s>0$, $|VU|=p>0$ (with $s,p<\pi$ when $\kappa=1$), $|WU|=q$, and angle $\theta$ at $V$; let $C_0\in[V,W]$ satisfy $|VC_0|=u$ with $0<u<s$. Then $|UC_0|$ is a strictly increasing function of $\theta\in[0,\pi]$: it is the third side of the model triangle with sides $p$ and $u$ meeting at the angle $\theta$, so the claim is the strict monotonicity in the included angle from [F2], applied with the fixed positive sides $p,u$. Consequently, if $V'W'U'$ is a second such triangle with $|V'W'|=s$, $|V'U'|=p$, $|W'U'|=q'\le q$, and marked point $C_0'\in[V'W']$ with $|V'C_0'|=u$, having angle $\theta'$ at $V'$, then $\theta'\le\theta$ by the strict monotonicity of the angle in the opposite side from [F2] (fixed sides $p,s$), hence $|U'C_0'|\le|UC_0|$. [F2, F3, algebra]

1.3 Reduction to an interior splitting point in (ii). If $r=q_0$ or $r=q_1$ then one of $\Delta_1,\Delta_2$ has a repeated vertex, its comparison triangle degenerates to a segment, the hypothesis for that index is vacuous, and the claim reduces to the hypothesis for the other index; so assume $r\in(q_0,q_1)$, which makes all six side lengths of $\Delta_1,\Delta_2$ positive, since $r\ne p$ and the vertices of $\Delta$ are distinct. [F4, given]

1.4 Local CAT angle comparison. For two unit-speed spherical rays meeting at angle $\theta$, let their points at distances $s,t>0$ with $s+t<\pi$ have distance $D$, and put $h=|s-t|$. The cosine rule and addition formulas give $4\sin^2(D/2)-4\sin^2(h/2)=2\sin s\sin t(1-\cos\theta)$. Factoring the left side yields $4\sin((D+h)/2)\sin((D-h)/2)$. With $\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin u/u$ for $u\ne0$ and $\operatorname{sinc}(0)=1$, it follows that $(D^2-h^2)/(2st)=(1-\cos\theta)\operatorname{sinc}(s)\operatorname{sinc}(t)/(\operatorname{sinc}((D+h)/2)\operatorname{sinc}((D-h)/2))$; when $D=h$, both sides are zero. Since $h\le D\le s+t$, [[cor-sin-x-over-x-limit]] makes the ratio tend uniformly to $1$ as $\max(s,t)\to0$, with no restriction on $s/t$. The Euclidean comparison cosine $1-(D^2-h^2)/(2st)$ thus tends to $\cos\theta$. In a CAT(1) triangle, CAT comparison bounds distances of arbitrarily short initial side points by these spherical model distances, hence bounds their Euclidean comparison angles by the model Euclidean angles. Taking the defining upper limit proves that each actual upper angle is at most its spherical model angle. The Euclidean case is the same cosine argument with the model angle constant. [F2, F3, F5, F7, algebra]

2.1 Local triangles for (iii). Apply a finite cover and the Lebesgue-number property of the compact square to the continuous map $c(s,t)=c_s(t)$. Choose partitions $s_i,t_j$ so that the image of each closed small rectangle is contained in a CAT($\kappa$) ball $U_{ij}$ of radius $<D_\kappa/4$ when $\kappa=1$, with its closure inside the corresponding local CAT chart. Such balls are geodesically convex: their intrinsic short geodesics are ambient minimizing segments, and distance from the center is convex in the Euclidean case and balls of radius $<\pi/2$ are convex in the spherical case by comparison with the convex model ball [F3]. Thus all restrictions of the radial geodesics and the last-row base segments remain in $U_{ij}$, and the joining geodesics chosen there are ambient geodesics. Put $L_j=c_{s_{i-1}}(t_j)$ and $R_j=c_{s_i}(t_j)$. For each strip take the triangle $(p,L_1,R_1)$ and, for $1\le j<n$, the two triangles $(L_j,R_j,R_{j+1})$ and $(L_j,L_{j+1},R_{j+1})$, choosing the horizontal and diagonal edges within the corresponding ball. Each of these $2n-1$ triangles lies in its local CAT ball and has comparison angles dominating its angles: apply the CAT inequality to arbitrarily short initial side points and take the upper-angle definition; the required uniform two-variable model-angle limit is established in step 1.4. In the Euclidean case the comparison angle is constant on short initial subsegments; in the spherical case that limit transfers the same bound to the Euclidean upper-angle convention. Coincident vertices contribute no angle obligation; collinear comparison triangles have angles $0,0,\pi$ and the same limiting inequalities apply. [step 1.4, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, construct]

2.2 Straightening construction. Extend the segment $[B,C]$ beyond $C$ by length $y$ to $B'_1$. Step 1.1 gives $u+y<\pi$ in the spherical case, so this extension remains a minimal arc; in both models $C\in[B,B'_1]$, $d(B,B'_1)=u+y$, and $\angle ACB'_1=\pi-\gamma$. [step 1.1, F1, F2, construct]

2.3 Perimeter bounds. The perimeter of each of $\Delta_1,\Delta_2$ is at most the perimeter of $\Delta$, which is $<2D_\kappa$, so the comparison triangles $\bar\Delta_1,\bar\Delta_2$ exist by [F3]; moreover $2d(q_0,q_1)\le d(q_0,q_1)+d(q_1,p)+d(p,q_0)$ and $2d(p,r)\le d(p,q_0)+d(p,q_1)+d(q_0,q_1)$ by the reverse triangle inequality applied to the two ends of $[q_0,q_1]$, so $d(q_0,q_1)<D_\kappa$ and $d(p,r)<D_\kappa$; in particular $d(\bar r,\bar q_0)+d(\bar r,\bar q_1)=d(q_0,q_1)<D_\kappa$ and $d(\bar p,\bar r)=d(p,r)<D_\kappa$, and the four boundary distances in (i) sum to the perimeter of $\Delta$, $<2D_\kappa$, as required. [step 1.3, F3, F4, algebra]

2.4 Angle triangle inequality and the splitting point. For three geodesics issuing from $O$, write $a,b$ for the upper angles between the first and middle, and middle and last. If $a+b\ge\pi$ their angle triangle inequality is automatic. Otherwise take $a_0>a$, $b_0>b$ with $a_0+b_0<\pi$. For sufficiently short endpoints at distances $s,t$ on the first and last geodesics, use the point at distance $v=st\sin(a_0+b_0)/(s\sin a_0+t\sin b_0)$ on the middle geodesic. This tends uniformly to zero with $\max(s,t)$, and the definition of upper angle bounds the two distances to that point by the Euclidean sides for included angles $a_0,b_0$. In the Euclidean triangle formed by rays at angles $a_0,b_0$ to their middle ray, that value of $v$ is the intersection of the middle ray with the side joining the endpoints; hence the sum of those two bounds is $\sqrt{s^2+t^2-2st\cos(a_0+b_0)}$. The metric triangle inequality and the law of cosines show that the comparison angle between the first and last endpoints is at most $a_0+b_0$. Taking the defining upper limit and then $a_0\downarrow a$, $b_0\downarrow b$ proves the angle triangle inequality. At $r$, the first and last segments are the opposite halves of $[q_0,q_1]$, of angle $\pi$, so the angles of $\Delta_1,\Delta_2$ there sum to at least $\pi$; their comparison angles therefore also sum to at least $\pi$. At $p$ the same triangle inequality bounds the angle of $\Delta$ by the sum of the two subtriangle angles. [step 1.3, F2, F4, F5, algebra, given]

3.1 The comparison step. In both models $d(A,B'_1)$ is the distance determined by the two sides $x=d(A,C)$ and $y=d(C,B'_1)$ and the included angle $\angle ACB'_1=\pi-\gamma$ at $C$, while $d(A,B')$ is determined by the same two sides and the included angle $\gamma'=\angle ACB'$; since $\gamma+\gamma'\ge\pi$ gives $\pi-\gamma\le\gamma'$, the strict monotonicity of the third side in the included angle from [F2] yields $d(A,B'_1)\le d(A,B')=q$, with equality if and only if $\gamma+\gamma'=\pi$. [step 2.2, F2, F3, algebra]

4.1 Proof of (1). By the triangle inequality and step 2.2, $d(B,A)+d(A,B'_1)\ge d(B,B'_1)=u+y$, and step 3.1 (together with $d(B,A)=p$) gives $d(B,A)+d(B',A)\ge d(B,A)+d(A,B'_1)\ge d(B,C)+d(C,B')$, which is (1). [step 2.2, step 3.1, F4]

4.2 Proof of (2): the distance assertion. Let $\Delta''$ be as in the Statement and put $x'':=d(\bar A,\bar C)$. The triangle $(A,B,B'_1)$ of steps 2.2 and 1.2 has $|AB|=p$, $|BB'_1|=u+y$, $|AB'_1|=d(A,B'_1)\le q$, and its marked point $C\in[B,B'_1]$ has $|BC|=u$; the triangle $(\bar B,\bar B',\bar A)$ has $|\bar B\bar B'|=u+y$, $|\bar B\bar A|=p$, $|\bar B'\bar A|=q$, and its marked point $\bar C\in[\bar B,\bar B']$ has $|\bar B\bar C|=u$. Both satisfy the hypotheses of step 1.2 with the same $s=u+y$ and $p$, the second with the larger opposite side, so $d(\bar A,\bar C)\ge d(A,C)=x$, with equality if and only if $d(A,B'_1)=q$, that is, if and only if $\gamma+\gamma'=\pi$ by step 3.1. [step 2.2, step 3.1, step 1.2, algebra]

5.1 Proof of (2): the angle at $\bar B'$. The triangles $(\bar A,\bar C,\bar B')$ and $(A,C,B')$ have two side lengths in common, $y=d(\bar C,\bar B')=d(C,B')$ and $q=d(\bar A,\bar B')=d(A,B')$, and their third sides are $x''$ and $x$; the angles $\bar\beta'$ and $\beta'$ lie opposite those third sides, so the strict monotonicity of the angle in the opposite side from [F2] gives $\bar\beta'\ge\beta'$, with strict inequality exactly when $x''>x$. [step 4.2, F2, algebra]

6.1 Proof of (2): the angle at $\bar A$. By step 1.1 the angle between $AB$ and $AB'$ is $\alpha+\alpha'\le\pi$ in both models. The triangles $(A,B,B')$ and $\Delta''$ have the same two adjacent sides $p,q$; their opposite sides are $d(B,B')$ and $s=u+y$. Since $d(B,B')\le s$, the law of cosines and its strict monotonicity give $\bar\alpha\ge\alpha+\alpha'$. Equality holds exactly when $d(B,B')=u+y$, equivalently $C\in[B,B']$, equivalently $\gamma+\gamma'=\pi$. Together with steps 4.2 and 5.1 this proves all three comparisons and simultaneous equality. [step 1.1, step 4.2, step 5.1, F2, F4, algebra]

7.1 Gluing and straightening. If one comparison triangle is collinear, use the closed cosine inequalities of (i), obtained from noncollinear model triangles by continuity of their side-length formulas; these inequalities remain valid when an included angle is $0$ or $\pi$, and no continuity of angles in the metric space is being assumed. Glue $\bar\Delta_1$ and $\bar\Delta_2$ along their common side $[\bar p,\bar r]$ so that $\bar q_0$ and $\bar q_1$ lie on opposite sides of the line through $\bar p$ and $\bar r$, which is possible because comparison triangles are unique up to isometry [F3]. In the glued configuration the four points $\bar p,\bar r,\bar q_0,\bar q_1$ are distinct, the points $\bar q_0,\bar q_1$ lie on opposite sides of the line through $\bar p$ and $\bar r$, the angles at $\bar r$ sum to at least $\pi$ by step 2.4, and the spherical perimeter hypothesis of clause (i) holds by step 2.3. Applying clause (i), whose clause (2) is established in steps 4.2, 5.1 and 6.1, with $(A,C,B,B')=(\bar p,\bar r,\bar q_0,\bar q_1)$ and then with $\bar q_0$ and $\bar q_1$ interchanged produces the comparison triangle $\Delta''=\Delta(\bar p,\bar q_0,\bar q_1)$ of $\Delta$ together with the point $\bar C\in[\bar q_0,\bar q_1]$ with $d(\bar q_0,\bar C)=d(q_0,r)$, and clause (2) gives: the angles of $\Delta''$ at $\bar q_0$ and at $\bar q_1$ are at least the comparison angles of $\bar\Delta_1,\bar\Delta_2$ at $\bar q_0,\bar q_1$; the angle of $\Delta''$ at $\bar p$ is at least the sum of those comparison angles at $\bar p$; and $d(\bar p,\bar C)\ge d(p,r)$, $\bar C$ being the point at distance $d(q_0,r)$ from $\bar q_0$ on the side $[\bar q_0,\bar q_1]$. [step 2.3, step 2.4, step 4.2, step 5.1, step 6.1, F3, algebra]

8.1 Conclusion of (ii). By step 7.1 the angles of the comparison triangle $\Delta''$ of $\Delta$ at $\bar q_0,\bar q_1$ dominate the comparison angles of $\bar\Delta_1,\bar\Delta_2$ at those vertices, which dominate the angles of $\Delta_1,\Delta_2$ there by the hypothesis of (ii), and the angle of $\Delta''$ at $\bar p$ dominates the sum of the comparison angles at $\bar p$, which dominates the angle of $\Delta$ at $p$; hence every vertex angle of the comparison triangle $\Delta''$ is at least the corresponding angle of $\Delta$. [step 7.1, step 2.4, given]

9.1 Assembling the strips. Starting with $(p,L_1,R_1)$, glue $(L_j,R_j,R_{j+1})$ along $L_jR_j$ and then $(L_j,L_{j+1},R_{j+1})$ along $L_jR_{j+1}$. The splitting points are respectively $R_j\in[p,R_{j+1}]$ and $L_j\in[p,L_{j+1}]$, so (ii) successively gives the angle comparisons for $(p,L_j,R_{j+1})$ and $(p,L_{j+1},R_{j+1})$. The perimeter of each such intermediate triangle is at most the full strip perimeter: bound its cross side by the remaining lengths on its two radial sides plus its final base side. The full strip perimeter is at most that of $\Delta$, by bounding both radial endpoint distances through the appropriate endpoints of the base. Thus every application has perimeter $<2D_\kappa$. Repeated or collinear triangles are removed or treated with the degenerate comparisons just described, and the same cosine inequalities extend to degenerate model triangles by continuity of the side-length formulas. Finally join the strips successively along $[p,\gamma(s_i)]$; now the splitting point is on the geodesic base and again each intermediate perimeter is at most the perimeter of $\Delta$. This proves (iii), and the last sentence follows by the same finite induction whenever its stated intermediate-triangle conditions hold. [step 2.1, step 2.4, step 8.1, F2, F3, F4, algebra] ∎

items.title: Berestovskii's cone criterion and the polyhedral link criterion
items.statement:
**(i) Berestovskii's theorem.** Let $L$ be a metric space, let $d_\pi:=\min\{\pi,d\}$, and let $C(L)=\{o\}\cup((0,\infty)\times L)$ be the Euclidean cone with the apex $o$ separately included and the metric $d_C(o,(r,x))=r$, $d_C^2((r,x),(s,y))=r^2+s^2-2rs\cos d_\pi(x,y)$ ([[def-cg-euclidean-cone-and-spherical-join-metrics]]). Then $C(L)$ is CAT(0) if and only if $(L,d_\pi)$ is CAT(1) ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]], [[lem-cg-comparison-convexity-and-model-spaces]]). With the convention $C(\varnothing)=\{o\}$, the empty link is CAT(1) vacuously and its cone is the one-point CAT(0) space, so the equivalence also covers $L=\varnothing$.

**(ii) Polyhedral link criterion.** Let $X$ be a connected isometric polyhedral gluing with finitely many shapes and local finiteness, with its chain metric ([[def-cg-abstract-isometric-polyhedral-gluing-and-chain-metric]], [[thm-cg-polyhedral-chain-metric-topology-and-properness]]), let $F$ be a $k$-dimensional face and let $p\in\operatorname{relint}F$. Then $X$ is locally CAT(0) at $p$ if and only if the angular link $\operatorname{Lk}_X(F)$, with its truncated metric, is CAT(1). A sufficiently small ball about $p$ is isometric to the ball of the same radius about $(0,o)$ in $\mathbb R^k\times C(\operatorname{Lk}_X(F))$ with the product metric ([[thm-cg-cone-join-metric-and-local-product-chart]]). In particular $X$ is locally CAT(0) if and only if the angular link of every vertex of $X$ is CAT(1).
items.strategy:
1.1 Cone geodesics and angular projections. The cone metric and the sector geodesics of [F1] apply to any truncated metric: their triangle-inequality proof uses only the triangle inequality and diameter bound of $d_\pi$. A minimizing segment from the apex is radial: for a point $(t,z)$ on it, equality $t+d_C((t,z),(r,x))=r$ and the cone formula force $z=x$ when $t>0$. On a minimizing cone segment from $(r,x)$ to $(s,y)$, $r,s>0$, a point $(t,z)$ satisfies equality in the triangle inequality. If $\alpha=d_\pi(x,z)$ and $\beta=d_\pi(z,y)$ have sum greater than $\pi$ and $t>0$, the strict cone triangle inequality proved in [F1] excludes equality. Otherwise develop the radii in the plane at angles $0,\alpha,\alpha+\beta$: the Euclidean triangle inequality and the decreasing cosine give the cone triangle inequality, and equality forces the developed middle point onto the straight endpoint segment. If $\gamma=d_\pi(x,y)<\pi$, equality also forces $\alpha+\beta=\gamma$, and the segment avoids the apex; its polar angle varies continuously and monotonically from $0$ to $\gamma$ (unless $\gamma=0$, when it is radial). The angular projection, parametrised by that angle, is a minimizing segment in $(L,d_\pi)$: apply the same equality argument to every subsegment. If $\gamma=\pi$, the developed segment is a diameter, so every nonapex point has direction $x$ or $y$ and the segment is the through-apex path. Assume now $C(L)$ is CAT(0). Its geodesics exist and are unique by [F5], so this argument gives existence of short angular segments; their uniqueness follows since two such segments would, by sector development, give two cone geodesics between the same positive-radius endpoints. [F1, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Forward comparison with the actual chord radii. Let a triangle of short angular segments in $L$ have perimeter $<2\pi$, and choose its spherical comparison triangle $(\bar y_1,\bar y_2,\bar y_3)$. Take cone vertices $P_i=s y_i$, $s>0$, and Euclidean vertices $\bar P_i=s\bar y_i\in\mathbb R^3$. Their pairwise distances agree by the cosine formula, so their affine plane is a Euclidean comparison triangle. If $y$ lies on an angular side, let $P=t y$ be the point on the corresponding cone geodesic whose angular projection is $y$, as supplied by step 1.1. Its radius $t$ is the radius of the point $\bar P=t\bar y$ on the corresponding straight chord: both sectors have the same opening angle, endpoint radii and polar position. In particular $P$ and $\bar P$ have the same side parameter; generally $t\ne s$. For any two points $y,y'$ on angular sides, use the corresponding chord points $P=t y$, $P'=t'y'$ and their comparison points. CAT(0) gives $t^2+t'^2-2tt'\cos d_\pi(y,y')\le|t\bar y-t'\bar y'|^2=t^2+t'^2-2tt'\cos d_S(\bar y,\bar y')$. Since $t,t'>0$, decreasing cosine on $[0,\pi]$ yields $d_\pi(y,y')\le d_S(\bar y,\bar y')$. With step 1.1 this proves CAT(1). [step 1.1, F1, F2, F5, algebra]

2.2 Reverse comparison, short angular perimeter. Assume $(L,d_\pi)$ is CAT(1). Short angular segments exist and are unique (the CAT(1) inequality on the degenerate triangle made from two competing short segments forces their equal-parameter points to coincide). Sector development and through-apex paths give cone geodesics, and step 1.1 classifies all of them. To prove CAT(0), use the squared vertex-to-side criterion of [[lem-cg-comparison-convexity-and-model-spaces]] (iv)(c). Fix a vertex $P_1=a y_1$, and a point $Q$ at fraction $v\in[0,1]$ of the side from $P_2=r y_2$ to $P_3=s y_3$. If $a=0$, the criterion is equality by the developed chord norm. If $r=0$ or $s=0$, the side is radial and the same equality follows by expanding the cone formula. Otherwise put $\alpha=d_\pi(y_1,y_2)$, $\beta=d_\pi(y_1,y_3)$ and $\gamma=d_\pi(y_2,y_3)$. For $\gamma=0$ the side is radial and again equality holds. Suppose $0<\gamma<\pi$ and write $Q=t y$ with angular position $\tau=d_\pi(y_2,y)$. In its developed sector, $$A:=\frac{(1-v)r}{t}=\frac{\sin(\gamma-\tau)}{\sin\gamma},\qquad B:=\frac{vs}{t}=\frac{\sin\tau}{\sin\gamma}.$$ If $\alpha+\beta+\gamma<2\pi$, the spherical comparison inequality gives $\cos d_\pi(y_1,y)\ge A\cos\alpha+B\cos\beta$, since the comparison direction at position $\tau$ is $A\bar y_2+B\bar y_3$. Expanding the cone formula therefore gives $$d_C(P_1,Q)^2\le(1-v)d_C(P_1,P_2)^2+v d_C(P_1,P_3)^2-v(1-v)d_C(P_2,P_3)^2.$$ [assume-case short, step 1.1, F1, F2, F3, algebra]

3.1 Reverse comparison, large angular perimeter. Retain $0<\gamma<\pi$ but suppose $\alpha+\beta+\gamma\ge2\pi$. Put $g(\tau)=A\cos\alpha+B\cos\beta$, $l=\pi-\alpha$ and $u=\beta+\gamma-\pi$, so $0\le l\le u\le\gamma$. Since $\beta\ge2\pi-\alpha-\gamma$ and $\alpha+\gamma\in[\pi,2\pi]$, reflection $\cos(\alpha+\gamma)=\cos(2\pi-\alpha-\gamma)$ and decreasing cosine on $[0,\pi]$ give $\cos\beta\le\cos(\alpha+\gamma)$; the addition formulas consequently give $g(\tau)\le\cos(\alpha+\tau)$ on $[0,l]$. Likewise $g(\tau)\le\cos(\beta+\gamma-\tau)$ on $[u,\gamma]$. In particular $g(l),g(u)\le-1$. If $l<u$, sine interpolation on this interval (length $u-l<\pi$) gives $$g(\tau)=\frac{\sin(u-\tau)}{\sin(u-l)}g(l)+\frac{\sin(\tau-l)}{\sin(u-l)}g(u)\le-1\qquad(l\le\tau\le u),$$ because the coefficients are nonnegative and their sum is $\cos(\tau-(l+u)/2)/\cos((u-l)/2)\ge1$; if $l=u$ use $g(l)\le-1$. The triangle inequality bounds $d_\pi(y_1,y)\le\min\{\pi,\alpha+\tau,\beta+\gamma-\tau\}$. Thus on the two outer intervals its cosine is at least the corresponding cosine above, and on the middle interval it is at least $-1\ge g(\tau)$. Hence $\cos d_\pi(y_1,y)\ge g(\tau)$ everywhere, and the expansion in step 2.2 proves the same squared comparison inequality. [assume-case large, step 2.2, F1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Reverse comparison, antipodal side. Suppose $\gamma=\pi$. Step 1.1 makes the side the through-apex path and the triangle inequality gives $\alpha+\beta\ge\pi$. Thus $\cos\alpha+\cos\beta=2\cos((\alpha+\beta)/2)\cos((\alpha-\beta)/2)\le0$. If $Q$ is on the $y_2$ branch, its radius is $t=r-v(r+s)\ge0$. The difference between the right side of the squared inequality in step 2.2 and $d_C(P_1,Q)^2$ is exactly $-2avs(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta)\ge0$, by expansion. On the $y_3$ branch it is $-2a(1-v)r(\cos\alpha+\cos\beta)\ge0$. Both include the apex. Together with the preceding two paragraphs, this case covers every side and every vertex; the vertex-to-side criterion [F3] therefore proves CAT(0), completing the reverse implication. [assume-case antipodal, step 1.1, step 2.2, step 3.1, F1, F2, F3, cases-exhaustive, algebra]

5.1 Cone equivalence. Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove the forward implication and steps 2.2, 3.1 and 4.1 the reverse implication, with the empty cone a single point. This proves (i) in full. [step 2.1, step 4.1]

6.1 Local charts and cone dilation. Put $Y=\mathbb R^k\times C(\operatorname{Lk}_X(F))$. By [F1], a small ball at $p$ is isometric to a ball at $(0,o)$ in $Y$. If $Y$ is CAT(0), its convex balls are CAT(0). Conversely if a ball about $(0,o)$ is CAT(0), the maps $(u,(r,x))\mapsto(\lambda u,(\lambda r,x))$, $\lambda>0$, are bijective similarities of $Y$, since both coordinate metrics scale by $\lambda$. Any two points can be scaled into that ball, joined there and scaled back, so $Y$ is geodesic; any chosen geodesic triangle is bounded and can likewise be scaled wholly into the ball, where its CAT(0) inequality holds, and scaled back. Thus local CAT(0) at the origin is equivalent to CAT(0) of $Y$. A square-sum product is CAT(0) when both factors are, by adding their squared vertex-to-side inequalities; conversely the slices of each factor are convex (a minimizing product segment with equal endpoints in one coordinate must keep that coordinate constant), so CAT(0) of the product implies CAT(0) of each factor. Since $\mathbb R^k$ is CAT(0), (i) now proves that $X$ is locally CAT(0) at $p$ exactly when its normal face link is CAT(1). [step 5.1, F1, F3, F5, algebra]

7.1 Vertex reduction. Necessity follows from step 6.1 with $F=\{v\}$. Conversely suppose every vertex link is CAT(1); then its entire cone is CAT(0) by step 5.1. For any point $p\in\operatorname{relint}F$, choose a vertex $v$ of $F$. In the tangent-cone gluing at $v$, the ray representing the cell segment from $v$ to $p$ has a point $q$ at small positive radius. Its incident cells are exactly those containing $F$: in every incident cell the relative interior of the ray is the relative interior of the tangent face corresponding to $F$. The active facet inequalities at $q$ are therefore precisely those containing $F$, the same as at $p$, and their Euclidean linear parts and gluing maps agree. Thus the tangent-cone gluing at $q$ is isometric to that at $p$. The finite-facet proof of the local chart [F4] applies equally to the finitely many incident polyhedral cones, so it identifies sufficiently small balls at both points with balls in this same tangent gluing (choose radii below the finitely many inactive facet distances, as in [F1]). Since the cone at $v$ is CAT(0), its small convex ball at $q$ is CAT(0), so the corresponding ball at $p$ is CAT(0). Hence $X$ is locally CAT(0) everywhere, proving the vertex form. [step 5.1, step 6.1, F1, F4, F5, algebra] ∎

items.title: Endpoint stability for local geodesics in complete locally CAT(0) spaces
items.strategy:
1.1 Convexity of balls in a CAT(0) space. Let $Y$ be CAT(0), $y_0\in Y$, $r>0$ and $u,v\in\bar B(y_0,r)$; let $m$ be a midpoint of the unique geodesic $[u,v]$. By [F2] the midpoint inequality gives $d(y_0,m)^2\le\tfrac12 d(y_0,u)^2+\tfrac12d(y_0,v)^2-\tfrac14d(u,v)^2\le r^2$, so $m\in\bar B(y_0,r)$; iterating the same computation for the midpoints of $[u,m]$ and $[m,v]$ and so on, every dyadic point of $[u,v]$ lies in $\bar B(y_0,r)$, and the dyadic points are dense in $[0,1]$, so continuity of the geodesic [F2] puts all of $[u,v]$ in $\bar B(y_0,r)$. Hence $\bar B(y_0,r)$ is convex. [F2, algebra]

2.1 A uniform radius. Consider all pairs $(t,r)$ with $r>0$ and $\bar B(c(t),r)$ CAT(0). Their open half-radius balls cover the compact image of $c$, so [F3] supplies finitely many $B(c(t_i),r_i/2)$ covering it, without choosing a radius at every point. Put $\varepsilon=\tfrac14\min_i r_i>0$. For every $t$, some $i$ has $d(c(t),c(t_i))<r_i/2$, and $2\varepsilon\le r_i/2$, so $\bar B(c(t),2\varepsilon)\subseteq\bar B(c(t_i),r_i)$. This ball is thus a ball in a CAT(0) space, hence complete (it is closed in the complete space $X$) and convex by step 1.1; in particular it is uniquely geodesic and has the convexity property [F2] for pairs of geodesics inside it. [step 1.1, F1, F2, F3]

3.1 Convexity tools. For geodesics $g,h$ in one CAT(0) chart, introduce the geodesic $k$ from $g(0)$ to $h(1)$: the common-initial-point estimate of [F2], followed by the same estimate on reversed geodesics, gives $d(g(t),h(t))\le t\,d(g(1),h(1))+(1-t)d(g(0),h(0))$. Apply this on every subinterval to obtain convexity of the distance function. A continuous locally convex real function on an interval is convex: on a sufficiently fine subdivision its consecutive secant slopes are nondecreasing by local convexity; summing the resulting inequalities gives the secant inequality for any three prescribed points. Consequently, for local geodesics $g,h$ satisfying $d(c(t),g(t)),d(c(t),h(t))<\varepsilon$, the function $d(g(t),h(t))$ is convex: near each parameter both curves are geodesics in the ball of step 2.1. Their distance is thus bounded by interpolation of endpoint distances, and they coincide if their endpoints coincide. A local geodesic whose entire image lies in one CAT(0) chart equals that chart's geodesic between its endpoints, by the same local-convexity argument with endpoint distances zero. [step 2.1, F2, algebra]

4.1 Initial existence. Let $P(A)$ mean that for every $[a,b]\subseteq[0,1]$ with $b-a<A$ and endpoints $u,v$ at distances $<\varepsilon$ from $c(a),c(b)$ there is a constant-speed local geodesic $g:[a,b]\to X$ with $d(c(t),g(t))<\varepsilon$ throughout. Take $A_0>0$ such that $\lambda A_0<\varepsilon$ (any $A_0$ if $\lambda=0$). Both endpoints then lie in $B(c(a),2\varepsilon)$; its geodesic joins them. The restriction of $c$ lies in that ball, hence is its geodesic by step 3.1. Convex separation bounds the distance between these two geodesics by the maximum of their endpoint distances, which is $<\varepsilon$. Thus $P(A_0)$ holds. [step 2.1, step 3.1, F4, choose]

4.2 Alternating-thirds construction. Suppose $P(A)$ and $b-a<3A/2$; set $a_1=a+(b-a)/3$ and $b_1=a+2(b-a)/3$. Put $p_0=c(a_1)$ and $q_0=c(b_1)$. For $n\ge1$, use $P(A)$ on $[a,b_1]$ and $[a_1,b]$ to obtain $g_n$ from $u$ to $q_{n-1}$ and $h_n$ from $p_{n-1}$ to $v$, and set $p_n=g_n(a_1)$, $q_n=h_n(b_1)$. Step 3.1 makes all these choices unique. Set $r=\max\{d(c(a),u),d(c(b),v)\}<\varepsilon$. Convexity shows inductively that each entire curve is within $r$ of $c$. It also gives $d(p_1,p_0),d(q_1,q_0)\le r/2$ and, for $n\ge1$, $d(p_{n+1},p_n)\le\tfrac12d(q_n,q_{n-1})$ and $d(q_{n+1},q_n)\le\tfrac12d(p_n,p_{n-1})$, since the evaluation points are halfway along their respective intervals and the other endpoints agree. Hence both increments at index $n$ are at most $r/2^n$. Both sequences are Cauchy, and completeness gives limits $p,q$ in the closed $r$-balls around $c(a_1),c(b_1)$. [assume-hyp, step 3.1, F6, construct, algebra]

5.1 Limits and overlap. Step 3.1 also gives $\sup d(g_{n+1},g_n)\le d(q_n,q_{n-1})$ and $\sup d(h_{n+1},h_n)\le d(p_n,p_{n-1})$; summing the geometric series yields uniform limits $g,h$. To verify they are local geodesics, fix a parameter and a small interval on which $c$ and all these curves lie in one ball of step 2.1, using the strict margin $r<\varepsilon$ and continuity of $c$. Each restricted curve is the chart's geodesic by step 3.1; the endpoint estimate there shows the limit is that geodesic too. Their speeds on overlapping such intervals agree, so each limit has a single constant speed. On $[a_1,b_1]$, the endpoints of $g$ and $h$ are $p,q$, so step 3.1 identifies them on the overlap. Their union is a constant-speed local geodesic on $[a,b]$ (if the overlap is constant, both speeds are zero). Its separation from $c$ is locally convex and therefore convex, bounded by the endpoint maximum $r$. This proves $P(3A/2)$. [step 3.1, step 4.2, F2, F5, F6]

6.1 Existence and uniqueness. Iteration yields $P((3/2)^kA_0)$ for all $k$; choose $k$ with $(3/2)^kA_0>1$ to obtain $c'$ on $[0,1]$. Step 3.1 makes its separation from $c$ convex and gives $d(c(t),c'(t))\le(1-t)d(c(0),x')+t\,d(c(1),y')<\varepsilon$. Conversely every candidate with convex separation has this bound, and step 3.1 identifies any two candidates with the same endpoints. [step 4.1, step 5.1, step 3.1, algebra]

7.1 Length with one endpoint fixed. Suppose $g,h$ are two solutions in this tube with $g(0)=h(0)$. For sufficiently small $t>0$ both initial restrictions are minimizing, so step 3.1 and the triangle inequality give $tL(h)=d(h(0),h(t))\le d(g(0),g(t))+d(g(t),h(t))\le tL(g)+t\,d(g(1),h(1))$. Divide by $t$ to obtain $L(h)\le L(g)+d(g(1),h(1))$. Let $k$ be the solution from $x'$ to $c(1)$ given by step 6.1. Apply this inequality first to the reversed curves $c,k$ and then to $k,c'$: $L(k)\le L(c)+d(c(0),x')$ and $L(c')\le L(k)+d(c(1),y')$. This is the asserted length bound. [step 3.1, step 6.1, F4, algebra]

8.1 Endpoint continuity. For solutions $c_n',c'$ in the same tube, step 3.1 gives $\sup_t d(c_n'(t),c'(t))\le\max\{d(x_n',x'),d(y_n',y')\}$. When the endpoints converge the right side tends to zero, which proves uniform convergence and clause (ii). [step 3.1, step 6.1, F6] ∎

items.title: The space of local geodesics, its length metric, and the covering criterion for local isometries
items.statement:
Let $X$ be a connected complete metric space that is locally CAT(0) and a length space ([[def-cg-cat-zero-cat-one-and-local-geodesic]]), let $x_0\in X$, and let $G_{x_0}$ be the set of constant-speed local geodesics $c:[0,1]\to X$ with $c(0)=x_0$, together with the constant path at $x_0$, carrying the sup metric $d_G(c,c')=\sup_{t\in[0,1]}d(c(t),c'(t))$ ([[def-topology-of-uniform-convergence]]). Then:

**(i)** $(G_{x_0},d_G)$ is complete; the truncation map $\Phi:G_{x_0}\times[0,1]\to G_{x_0}$, $\Phi(c,s)(t):=c(st)$, is continuous and contracts $G_{x_0}$ to the constant path, so $G_{x_0}$ is contractible and simply connected ([[def-nullhomotopic-map-and-contractible-space]], [[def-simply-connected]]).

**(ii)** The endpoint evaluation $\exp:G_{x_0}\to X$, $\exp(c):=c(1)$, is a local isometry: for every $c$ there is $\rho>0$ such that $\exp$ restricts to an isometry of the $\rho$-ball about $c$ onto the $\rho$-ball about $c(1)$ in $X$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]], [[def-metric-ball]]).

**(iii)** Define $\hat d(c,c')$ to be the infimum of $L_{d_G}(\eta)$ over continuous paths $\eta:[0,1]\to G_{x_0}$ from $c$ to $c'$, where length is computed in the metric $d_G$ ([[lem-cg-metric-target-length-reparametrization-and-lower-semicontinuity]]). With this induced length metric, $(G_{x_0},\hat d)$ is a complete length space, $\hat d$ induces the same topology as $d_G$, and $\exp:(G_{x_0},\hat d)\to X$ is a local isometry and a covering map ([[def-covering-map-and-evenly-covered-neighbourhoods]]); in particular $\exp$ is surjective and $(G_{x_0},\hat d)$ is a universal covering space of $X$ ([[def-universal-covering-space]]).

**(iv) Metric covering criterion.** Let $Y$ be a nonempty connected complete metric space, let $Z$ be a connected locally uniquely geodesic metric space whose local geodesics vary continuously with their endpoints (on a sufficiently small convex neighbourhood of each point, the constant-speed segments depend continuously in the uniform metric on both endpoints), and let $f:Y\to Z$ be a local isometry; then $f$ is a covering map. More precisely, $f$ is surjective, and every $z\in Z$ has a uniquely geodesic neighbourhood $U$ over which the fibres of $f$ are discrete and $f$ restricts to a homeomorphism on a disjoint family of open sheets.
items.strategy:
1.1 Completeness of the sup metric. For $c,c'\in G_{x_0}$, $d(c(t),c'(t))\le L(c)+L(c')$, so the supremum defining $d_G$ is finite; separation and symmetry follow pointwise, and taking suprema in the pointwise triangle inequality proves its triangle inequality. Convergence in $d_G$ is exactly uniform convergence. Let $(c_n)$ be uniformly Cauchy. Completeness of $X$ gives a uniform continuous limit $c$ with $c(0)=x_0$. Near any parameter, choose a closed CAT(0) ball centred at $c(t)$ and a nontrivial parameter interval on which $c$ lies strictly inside that ball. Uniform convergence puts every sufficiently late $c_n$ on this interval inside the same ball. Each restricted $c_n$ is that chart's geodesic, by the local-convexity argument proved in [F1]. Therefore $d(c_n(u),c_n(v))=L(c_n)|u-v|$ throughout that interval. Fix two distinct parameters there: their converging chord lengths show that $L(c_n)$ has a finite limit $\lambda$. Passing the distance equality to the limit on each such interval gives $d(c(u),c(v))=\lambda|u-v|$ locally with the same $\lambda$ throughout. Thus $c\in G_{x_0}$, and it is the sup-metric limit. [F1, F2, F5]


1.2 Contraction. Truncations $\Phi(c,s)(t)=c(st)$ belong to $G_{x_0}$, including the constant path at $s=0$, and $d_G(\Phi(c,s),\Phi(c',s'))\le d_G(c,c')+L(c')|s-s'|$. This proves joint continuity at each $(c',s')$, and $\Phi(c,0)$ is constant while $\Phi(c,1)=c$. This contraction shows contractibility directly: for every continuous map $f:G_{x_0}\to Z$, composition $f\circ\Phi$ is a homotopy from a constant to $f$. For a loop $\beta$ based at any $a\in G_{x_0}$, put $H(c,s)=\Phi(c,1-s)$ and $a_s(u)=H(a,su)$. The loops $a_s*(H(\beta(-),s))*\bar a_s$, using three equal parameter pieces, form a continuous based homotopy from $\beta$ with constant pauses to $a_1*\bar a_1$ with a constant middle piece. Pauses are removed by linear reparametrization, and the latter retracing loop contracts by replacing $a_1$ with $u\mapsto a_1((1-v)u)$, $0\le v\le1$, on both halves. Every basepoint therefore has trivial fundamental group; the truncation paths also give path connectedness. Thus $G_{x_0}$ is simply connected without a change-of-basepoint theorem. [F1, F4, F5, algebra]

1.3 The evaluation chart. Fix $c$ and an endpoint-stability radius $\varepsilon$. Each endpoint $y$ with $d(y,c(1))<\varepsilon$ has a solution $c_y$ from $x_0$ satisfying $d_G(c,c_y)<\varepsilon$. Conversely any local geodesic $g$ with $d_G(g,c)<\varepsilon$ has locally convex, hence convex, separation from $c$, so uniqueness in [F1] identifies it with $c_{g(1)}$. For any two chart solutions the same pair-convexity gives $d(c_y(t),c_z(t))\le t\,d(y,z)$. Evaluating at $t=1$ yields exactly $d_G(c_y,c_z)=d(y,z)$. Thus evaluation is an isometry between the open $\varepsilon$-balls. Smaller closed balls are identified as well, giving the corresponding closed-ball convention. [F1, F2, F5]

1.4 A covering criterion with continuous radial geodesics. First consider a nonempty complete connected locally geodesic metric space $Y$, a connected locally uniquely geodesic metric space $Z$ whose local geodesics depend continuously on endpoints, and a local isometry $f:Y\to Z$. Any finite-length path in $Z$ has a unique lift from a prescribed initial point of its fibre: inverse charts give the lift until its supremal parameter, and preservation of length makes the lifted tail Cauchy, so completeness and one more inverse chart extend it. Uniqueness follows because two lifts agreeing at a parameter agree near it, and the agreement set is closed. Any two points of $Z$ can be joined by a finite concatenation of short geodesics: the set reachable from a fixed point and its complement are open, hence connectedness makes the former all of $Z$. Choose $y_0\in Y$; lifting such paths from $f(y_0)$ proves surjectivity. Choose an open uniquely geodesic ball $U$ at $z$. For each $y\in f^{-1}(z)$ lift its radial geodesics and denote their endpoints by $s_y(w)$. These endpoints depend continuously on $w$: cover each fixed lifted radial path by finitely many inverse charts and subdivide its parameter; continuity of the radial paths keeps nearby radial paths in the same chart images, and successive inverse charts prove uniform continuity of their lifts near the fixed path. Thus $s_y$ is continuous and $f\circ s_y=\mathrm{id}_U$. Near each $s_y(w)$, continuity and the inverse chart show that $s_y$ equals the local inverse of $f$, so its image is open. Distinct sections have disjoint images, since lifting the reversed radial path from a common endpoint would give the same starting fibre point. Every point over $U$ lies in a section, by lifting that reversed path first. These sections are precisely the required evenly covered sheets. [F2, F3, F4, F5, construct]

2.1 The length metric. For $s,s'\in[0,1]$, $d_G(\Phi(c,s),\Phi(c,s'))\le L(c)|s-s'|$, so the contraction supplies finite-length paths to the constant path and $\hat d$ is finite. Always $\hat d\ge d_G$. In an evaluation chart, join sufficiently close endpoints by the geodesic in the convex CAT(0) ball. Its inverse chart path has the same length, and hence $\hat d=d_G$ for pairs in a sufficiently small concentric ball. The metrics thus have the same topology. A $\hat d$-Cauchy sequence has a $d_G$-limit by step 1.1; eventually it and its limit lie in such a smaller ball, where equality implies convergence also in $\hat d$. Therefore $\hat d$ is complete and evaluation remains a local isometry. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, F2, F3, F5]

3.1 Application to (i)–(iii). Apply step 1.4 to $Y=(G_{x_0},\hat d)$ and $Z=X$: steps 1.3 and 2.1 supply local geodesicity, completeness and the local isometry, and $X$ has convex CAT(0) balls with continuously varying geodesics by [F2]. The contraction in step 1.2 makes $Y$ connected and simply connected. Evaluation is therefore a surjective covering and a universal covering. This proves (i)–(iii) without invoking the stronger clause (iv). [step 1.2, step 1.3, step 2.1, step 1.4, F2, F4]

4.1 General criterion (iv). A local isometry from $Y$ to $Z$ identifies a neighbourhood of each point of $Y$ with a neighbourhood in $Z$. Shrinking further to a convex geodesic neighbourhood in $Z$ makes $Y$ locally geodesic, so step 1.4 applies directly to the hypotheses of (iv). Its radial sections prove precisely the asserted surjectivity, discreteness of fibres and open disjoint sheets, without requiring either ambient metric to be a global length metric. [step 1.4, F4, F5] ∎
